motion: Does suffering provide evidence against theism?

bridges.description: Show that suffering is evidentially more expected on indifference than on classical theism.
Defend the conditional likelihood premises that generate the comparative inference.
Argue that enriched theistic explanations incur prior-probability costs unless independently supported.
Identify apparently purposeless suffering that soul-making does not predict well.
Challenge appeals to unknown divine reasons as unsupported possibility.
Maintain that basic moral knowledge survives acknowledged cognitive limits.
Compare suffering worlds with available non-suffering alternatives that may realize the same goods.
Show that the force of suffering depends on the broader theistic background against which it is conditioned.
Concede the genuine problem under classical attributes without abandoning them.
Explain why moral formation makes some suffering expected on a richer theistic view.
Frame the issue as whether suffering defeats an already-held and independently supported worldview.
Identify established theistic resources addressing animal and natural suffering.
Argue that finite agents lack access to the full range of possible divine reasons.
Use permissible-suffering cases and fallible first-person testimony to caution against sharp thresholds.

sections.rationale: Preserves the extended dispute over background packages, entailment, and Rauser's qualified concession about bare theism.

sections.title: Animal suffering and independent support
sections.rationale: Examines whether natural suffering remains unexplained and whether resurrection-style auxiliaries have prior support.

sections.title: Cognitive closure and moral knowledge
sections.rationale: Pairs limited access to divine reasons with Malpass's claim that extreme cases remain morally intelligible.

sections.title: Thresholds, testimony, and counterfactual lives
sections.rationale: Separates the threshold exchange, trauma testimony, fallibility, and the whole-life counterfactual challenge.

sections.title: World-level effects and the caregiving example
sections.rationale: Captures the final dispute over unknown global effects, an actual family causal history, and non-suffering alternatives.
